summary: Defines a framework for standardizing metrics of bulk transport capacity, which is how much data a single congestion-controlled connection can move. It aims to cover the variety of transport behaviors.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a plan for measuring how much a single big delivery can carry along a road.

questions: how is bulk transfer capacity defined
subtitle: A rulebook for measuring how fast one well-behaved TCP-style connection can move bulk data across a network path.

tldr.problem: Bulk Transport Capacity (BTC) is meant to measure how fast a single congestion-aware connection can move data, but the congestion control algorithms IETF standards permit differ enough that two tools can report non-comparable numbers.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines BTC as data_sent / elapsed_time, requires each BTC metric to be specified much more tightly than a typical protocol, and asks every methodology to collect ancillary metrics that help explain its results.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework, not a metric itself: each concrete BTC metric must fill in the details it lists, and the document says the framework may need revisiting as congestion control evolves.

facts.label: Data counted
facts.value: Unique data bits only, no headers, retransmissions once

facts.label: Must implement
facts.value: Slow start, congestion avoidance, retransmission timeout

sections.title: What Bulk Transport Capacity Means
sections.content:
Bulk Transport Capacity (BTC) is a measure of a network's ability to transfer significant quantities of data with a single congestion-aware transport connection, such as TCP. The intuitive definition is the expected long-term average data rate, in bits per second, of a single ideal TCP implementation over the path in question.

The RFC says this matters because for applications such as FTP, and the web when delivering large images or documents, BTC dominates the elapsed time and so the performance the user perceives. The metric a tool MUST report is BTC = data_sent / elapsed_time, where data_sent counts only unique data bits. Header bits are not counted, and a retransmitted packet's data is counted once.
sections.plainLanguage: BTC is the speed you get when one big download runs for a long time. You only count the real stuff you wanted, not the packaging, and not the same thing twice.

sections.title: Why Standardizing the Metric Is Hard
sections.content:
Central to BTC is the idea that all transport protocols should respond to congestion in similar ways. RFC 2581 sets the standard congestion control algorithms for TCP, but it permits considerable latitude, by design, to encourage evolution. That diversity is enough that different implementations can give non-comparable measures and potentially fail the formal tests for being a metric.

The RFC adds that most TCP implementations show non-linear performance over part of their operating region. It is possible to build simple simulations where raising a link's data rate lowers overall TCP throughput. The authors see this as a weakness in current understanding of congestion control, and note that new experimental algorithms and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) might affect BTC metrics, so the framework may need to be revisited.

Two approaches answer the problem. Each BTC metric must be much more tightly specified than a typical IETF protocol, and each methodology is expected to collect ancillary metrics, or enough data (for example a segment trace) to derive them.
sections.plainLanguage: Different trucks may brake and speed up in different ways, so their trip times are not fair to compare. The fix is to write the driving rules down very exactly and keep notes about the road.

sections.title: Congestion Control Rules a Metric Must Pin Down
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC lists five standard congestion control algorithms: Congestion Avoidance, Retransmission timeouts, Slow-start, Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery. All BTC implementations MUST implement slow start and congestion avoidance as in RFC 2581. They SHOULD implement fast retransmit and fast recovery, and MUST implement a retransmission timeout.

Because that RFC leaves choices open, every BTC methodology MUST define these details:

  • the algorithm used to increase cwnd during congestion avoidance;
  • which increase algorithm applies when cwnd equals ssthresh;
  • any advanced loss recovery (such as NewReno or SACK-based) in full;
  • the segment size or how it is chosen (for example path MTU discovery), the header bytes assumed per segment, and whether the size is artificially limited;
  • how the retransmission timeout is calculated, when the clock is set and the clock granularity (see RFC 2988).

New algorithms placed on the standards track may be incorporated, but the implementation decisions of the relevant RFCs SHOULD be fully specified in the metric.
sections.plainLanguage: Every team measuring must write down their exact driving rules: how fast to speed up, how to react to a bump, and how long to wait before trying again.

sections.title: Ancillary Metrics
sections.content:
Section 3 RECOMMENDS that ancillary metrics be built into each BTC methodology, or that enough information be provided (such as a segment trace) to derive them afterwards. They help corroborate the direct result against analytical models and diagnose why different methodologies disagree.

  • Congestion Avoidance Capacity (CAC): the data rate of a fully specified Congestion Avoidance algorithm when Retransmission Timeout and Slow-Start are not invoked. It has no meaning across timeouts or slow-start periods. It would be an ideal BTC metric in principle, but timeouts and slow-start recovery are prevalent on the Internet and should be captured.
  • Self-clock preservation: transitions between timer-driven and ACK-clocked operation SHOULD be instrumented. This covers lost transmission opportunities, loss of an entire window (BTC metrics SHOULD report it), algorithms that sustain the clock (which MUST be documented) and false timeouts.
  • Path properties: BTC metrics SHOULD instrument packet reordering (slightly, sufficiently and far out of order) and the maximum cwnd seen in congestion avoidance and slow start.
  • Calibration checks: any packets dropped inside the sending host MUST be reported, and the host's maximum queue lengths SHOULD be instrumented, to show the test platform is not the bottleneck.
  • Other: report whether advanced TCP extensions would be needed to match the BTC, and separate forward and reverse path properties where possible, instrumenting reverse-path load if not.
sections.plainLanguage: Along with the speed number, you keep a diary: how often the truck stalled, whether boxes arrived out of order, and whether your own loading dock was the slow part.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security, but metrics built on it may. Because BTC metrics try to fill a bottleneck link, and the connection may not use TCP packets, a test may look like a denial of service attack to network operators. Administrators of the source, destination and intervening networks may wish to make agreements about timing, size and frequency of tests.

Metrics generate their own packets rather than sampling user data, so they do not threaten user data confidentiality. Test packets might be identified and treated differently, or fake packets injected, which could distort results; packet interference checks such as a cryptographic hash may help. There are no IANA considerations for the framework itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A speed test pushes as hard as it can, so a network owner might mistake it for an attack. People should agree on when to run tests, and the test should be protected from tampering.
